claims.text: The initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu exhibit differential atomic-diffusion behavior in the alloy.
Differential diffusion during heating produces local compositional segregation in the nanoparticles.
Heating produces compositional fluctuations and incipient phase segregation at particle surfaces and cores.
Copper preferentially accumulates in specific nanoparticle regions during heating.
Copper is a relatively low-melting constituent of this alloy.
Copper-enriched regions have a reduced local melting point.
The reduced local melting point of segregated regions causes localized premelting before the entire nanoparticle melts.
Single-metal and binary-alloy nanoparticle baselines generally have more uniform diffusion rates.
Simpler metallic nanoparticles generally melt more homogeneously than the proposed high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Simpler metallic nanoparticles have a higher and sharper premelting onset than the proposed high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will show liquid-like regions correlated with low-melting-element enrichment below the bulk melting point.
Compositional segregation will depress and broaden the premelting onset.
The proposed mechanism applies to similarly composed nanoparticles with sizes of tens of nanometers under rapid heating in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
Oxidation or substrate interactions can dominate the thermal response and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Variability in diffusion kinetics and nanoparticle size dispersion affects the premelting-temperature shift and spatial extent of segregation.
